Bootstrap Standard Errors for Inverse Probability Weighted Analyses

Source: R/ipwboot.R
ipwboot.Rd

Bootstraps a whole inverse probability weighted analysis: in each bootstrap sample the weights are re-estimated and the marginal structural model is refitted, so the standard error accounts for the uncertainty in the estimated weights. For data in long format (several rows per subject), whole subjects are resampled and each sampled copy gets a new identifier.

Usage

ipwboot(data, statistic, id = NULL, R = 200, strata = NULL, conf = 0.95, ...)

# S3 method for class 'ipwboot'
print(x, digits = 4, ...)

# S3 method for class 'ipwboot'
confint(object, parm, level = object$conf, ...)

Arguments

data

Data frame with the original data.

statistic

Function that takes a data frame (a bootstrap sample of data) as its first argument and returns a numeric vector of estimates, for example the coefficients of a weighted outcome model. It should compute the weights itself, e.g. by calling ipwpoint or ipwtm.

id

Optional name of the subject identifier column (unquoted or as a string). If given, subjects are resampled with all their rows, and in each bootstrap sample the column is replaced by new identifiers 1, 2, ..., one per sampled copy, so that a subject drawn twice counts as two subjects. If NULL, rows are resampled.

R

Number of bootstrap samples. About 200 are usually enough for a standard error; use more (e.g. 1000) for percentile confidence intervals.

strata

Optional name of a column (unquoted or as a string) defining strata; resampling is then done within each stratum, keeping the number of subjects (or rows) per stratum fixed. With id, the column must be constant within each subject.

conf

Confidence level of the percentile intervals.

...

Further arguments passed to statistic; for the methods, ignored.

x, object

An object of class "ipwboot".

digits

Number of significant digits to print.

parm

Estimates (names or positions) for which to give intervals; all by default.

level

Confidence level.

Value

A list of class "ipwboot" containing:

t0

Estimates from the original data.

t

Matrix of bootstrap estimates, one row per bootstrap sample (NA for failed samples).

se

Bootstrap standard errors.

ci

Percentile confidence intervals.

R, conf

Number of bootstrap samples and confidence level.

n.fail

Number of failed bootstrap samples.

errors

Distinct error messages of failed samples.

id, strata

Names of the identifier and strata columns, if used.

call

The original function call.

Details

Austin (2016) found in simulations that, for weighted Cox models, naive standard errors were too small and robust (sandwich) standard errors too large, while the bootstrap in which the weights are re-estimated in each sample gave correct standard errors and confidence intervals. Austin studied a point treatment with baseline confounders; for longitudinal data the same idea applies with subjects as the resampling unit.

Bootstrap samples in which statistic fails, or returns a result of a different length, are left out of the summaries; their number is reported. Use set.seed() before calling ipwboot to make the results reproducible.

References

Austin, P.C. (2016). Variance estimation when using inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) with survival analysis. Statistics in Medicine, 35, 5642-5655. doi:10.1002/sim.7084 .

See also

ipwpoint, ipwtm.

Author

Hung Thai Tran hungtt@oucru.org

Examples

# Point treatment: true causal effect of a on y is 10
set.seed(16)
n <- 500
simdat <- data.frame(l = rnorm(n, 10, 5))
simdat$a <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(simdat$l - 10))
simdat$y <- 10 * simdat$a + 0.5 * simdat$l + rnorm(n, -10, 5)

msm.effect <- function(d) {
  w <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = d)$ipw.weights
  coef(lm(y ~ a, data = d, weights = w))["a"]
}
set.seed(1)
res <- ipwboot(simdat, msm.effect, R = 50)  # use about 200 in practice
res
#> Bootstrap of an inverse probability weighted analysis
#> 50 bootstrap samples, resampling rows
#> 
#>   estimate     se 2.5 % 97.5 %
#> a    11.41 0.8103 10.19  12.94
confint(res)
#>      2.5 %   97.5 %
#> a 10.18977 12.93739

# \donttest{
# Time-varying treatment: resample patients, re-estimate both weights
data(haartdat)
haart.effect <- function(d) {
  w1 <- ipwtm(exposure = haartind, family = "survival", numerator = ~ sex + age,
              denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt, id = patient,
              tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "first", data = d)
  w2 <- ipwtm(exposure = dropout, family = "survival", numerator = ~ sex + age,
              denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt, id = patient,
              tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "cens", data = d)
  fit <- survival::coxph(survival::Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ haartind,
                         data = d, weights = w1$ipw.weights * w2$ipw.weights)
  coef(fit)
}
set.seed(2)
ipwboot(haartdat, haart.effect, id = patient, R = 20)  # use about 200 in practice
#> Bootstrap of an inverse probability weighted analysis
#> 20 bootstrap samples, resampling subjects ('patient')
#> 
#>          estimate    se  2.5 %  97.5 %
#> haartind  -0.9363 0.362 -1.495 -0.2691
# }
